JSON: Name: sebaceous_tumour_integrative_pipeline Title: An integrative whole-exome and transcriptome computational pipeline to predict mismatch repair deficiency and molecular subtypes in sebaceous tumours Short Hypothesis: An integrative model that combines whole-exome sequencing indel burden, mutational signature decomposition, somatic copy-number features and tumor RNA expression will predict mismatch repair deficiency and Lynch-syndrome-associated germline variants in sebaceous tumours with higher sensitivity and specificity than classifiers based on tumor mutational burden or immunohistochemistry alone. Related Work: Existing studies have profiled sebaceous tumours using targeted panels, whole-exome sequencing, and limited transcriptomics to identify recurrent drivers (NOTCH1, RREB1, HRAS, TP53), SCNAs (1q21.3, 8q, 20), and mutational signatures linked to dMMR, UV, POLE/POLD1 and AID/APOBEC. Prior analytic approaches rely on single-modality predictors (TMB, IHC, or single-signature presence) or small-cohort descriptive clustering; mutational-signature methods and indel-rate thresholds have been proposed to infer dMMR but are pipeline-dependent and not validated in large, multi-centre ST cohorts. Integrative latent-variable clustering (MOFA-style) has been applied in other tumour types to define molecular subtypes but has not been systematically benchmarked against clinical MMR/IHC/germline data in sebaceous tumours. Limitations in prior work include small sample sizes for peri-ocular SC, variable FFPE-derived data quality, lack of comprehensive ablation comparing WES-only, RNA-only and combined models, absence of external validation cohorts, and unresolved dependence of indel-rate thresholds and signature calls on variant-calling pipelines. Abstract: Diagnosing mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR) and identifying Lynch-syndrome-associated cases among sebaceous tumours is clinically important but challenging due to tumour rarity, histological overlap and variable assay availability. We propose an integrative computational pipeline that ingests whole-exome sequencing and tumor RNA-seq to derive indel burden, de novo mutational signatures, allele-specific somatic copy-number profiles, driver mutation calls and expression-based latent factors, and then combines these features in machine-learning models to predict dMMR status and prioritize patients for germline testing. The pipeline also performs integrative clustering to define reproducible molecular subtypes and outputs driver/neoantigen annotations for translational hypothesis generation. The main contribution is a validated, modality-aware classifier and a modular analysis workflow that quantifies how much each data modality contributes to dMMR and Lynch prediction, and that provides subtype labels linked to clinically actionable genomic events. Expected outcomes include higher diagnostic sensitivity and specificity for dMMR/Lynch detection compared with TMB- or IHC-only approaches and a reproducible molecular taxonomy of sebaceous tumours to guide clinical triage and research. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset: 197 primary sebaceous tumours with matched normal WES; subset: 170 tumours with matched tumor RNA-seq; full cohort available: 286 tumours (use for additional exploratory analyses). External validation cohorts: TCGA skin cohorts (SKCM and, where applicable, SCC) and published MSK-IMPACT or equivalent public skin/exome datasets filtered to non-melanoma cases; at least one independent set with WES+matched-normal required. Preprocessing: standardize variant calling (BWA-MEM alignment, CaVEMan+Pindel or Mutect2/Strelka2+Manta for somatic calls), ASCAT for allele-specific SCNAs, SigProfilerExtractor for SBS/DBS/ID signatures, STAR+HTSeq for expression, MOFA-derived latent factors for integrative features. Gold-standard labels: dMMR defined by concordant loss of MMR protein by IHC and biallelic MMR inactivation where available; Lynch germline status defined by validated constitutional pathogenic variants. Primary prediction task: binary dMMR classification; secondary task: prioritize patients for germline testing (binary). Baselines: (1) IHC MMR (clinical gold standard when available), (2) TMB-based classifier (continuous TMB threshold based), (3) indel-rate threshold classifier (pipeline-specific threshold e.g. >0.345 indels/Mb), (4) mutational-signature-only classifier (presence of SBS15/20/ID7), (5) WES-only machine learning (no RNA features), (6) RNA-only classifier (expression latent factors only). Models: logistic regression with L2, random forest, XGBoost; hyperparameter search via nested 5-fold CV. Train/validation/test: stratified by ST subtype and sequencing center; 60/20/20 split, plus 5× repeated stratified cross-validation for robustness. Evaluation metrics: AUROC, AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, F1, balanced accuracy; calibration (Brier score); decision-curve net benefit for germline referral threshold. Statistical tests: DeLong test for AUROC comparisons, McNemar’s for paired sensitivity/specificity, bootstrap (n=1000) for CIs. Ablation studies: compare full integrative model vs (a) drop RNA, (b) drop SCNA features, (c) drop mutational signatures, (d) use TMB instead of indel-rate; report delta-AUROC and 95% CI. Additional analyses: (i) clustering evaluation—compute silhouette score and adjusted Rand index against histopathological labels and IHC groupings; (ii) survival/prognostic association—Cox proportional hazards and log-rank for recurrence/metastasis using molecular subtypes; (iii) neoantigen-immunity correlation—compute CSiN neoantigenicity and correlate (Spearman) with EPIC/ TIMER CD8+ and CD4+ fractions and report p-values corrected by Benjamini-Hochberg; (iv) driver-call concordance—Jaccard index comparing dNdScv and OncodriveFML calls. Robustness checks: center-holdout validation, tumor-only (no matched normal) mode evaluation, and sensitivity of indel threshold when using alternative variant callers. Computational environment: Linux cluster, 64 CPU cores, 512 GB RAM, GPU optional for deep models. Reproducibility: containerized workflow (Nextflow or Snakemake), fixed random seeds and documented software versions. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data quality and FFPE artifacts: variable DNA/RNA quality and low input from FFPE samples can generate false-positive/negative calls and bias indel and signature estimates. Pipeline dependence: indel-rate thresholds and signature decomposition are sensitive to variant-calling and filtering choices; models may not generalize across pipelines. Cohort bias and power: peri-ocular SC-O is underrepresented, limiting statistical power for that subtype and for rare germline variants; geographic and ancestry skew (Europe/Asia) may reduce generalizability. Tumor heterogeneity and clonality: subclonal mutations and cnLOH can mislead biallelic inactivation calls and neoantigen clonality estimates. Tumor-only sequencing mode: absence of matched normal increases germline-somatic ambiguity and false positives in driver and signature calls. Signature deconvolution limits: low-mutation samples (pauci-mutated tumors) produce unstable signature assignments. Clinical translation limits: predicted Lynch association requires confirmatory germline testing; classifier false positives could generate unnecessary referrals. Computational cost and scalability: full integrative analysis (WES+RNA+ASCAT+SigProfiler+MOFA) is resource-intensive and may be impractical for low-resource settings. Immunogenicity prediction uncertainty: neoantigen binding and immunogenicity metrics (CSiN) do not reliably predict clinical response to immunotherapy.
